title: Beyond Linear Processing: Dendritic Bilinear Integration in Spiking Neural Networks
claim: A single neuron with correlation-sensitive integration solves a nonlinear task that the standard linear-summation neuron cannot.
layout: 5 panels: neuron and XOR schematic top-left, heatmaps below, spike/trace plots right
description: Five-panel figure. Panel A shows a drawn dendritic neuron with blue arrows (pathway 1) and red arrows (pathway 2) pointing at the dendrites. Panel B is a 2x2 XOR truth table, with pathway 1 on the x-axis and pathway 2 on the y-axis. Spike icons mark the on/off and off/on cells, and circled numbers 1–3 label the patterns. Panels C and D are two 10x10 viridis correlation heatmaps with a block structure. Panel E, the largest, has three boxed columns for patterns 1–3. Each column has a spike raster on top (blue for pathway 1, red for pathway 2). Below it are membrane potential traces, with green for LIF and orange for DLIF. DLIF stays silent for pattern 1, while LIF still fires. Pathway brackets and a legend sit at the right.
caption: A single DLIF model can effectively solve the XOR problem. (A): A neuron receives inputs from two distinct pathways (represented in blue and red), each containing five synaptic inputs. (B): The XOR operation schematic: the neuron remains inactive when both pathways are on or off, but it fires when only one pathway is on, thereby implementing the XOR operation. It is trivial that the neuron is inactive when both pathways are off. Therefore, we only consider the other three input patterns, which are labeled as 1⃝, 2⃝, and 3⃝, respectively. (C): Expectation of the normalized difference in correlation matrices between two classes C1−C2 ∥C1−C2∥F . (D): Expectation of the bilinear coefficient K for the DLIF neuron. (E): Three different patterns in the XOR problem. Pathway 1 includes synapse indices 1-5, while pathway 2 includes synapse indices 6-10. The DLIF model keeps silent when both pathways are activated (labeled as 1⃝) and fires when receiving input patterns with only one pathway is activated (labeled as 2⃝and 3⃝), thus achieving the XOR operation (orange). In contrast, the LIF model still fires when both pathways are active (labeled as 1⃝), thus it is unable to perform the XOR operation.
abstract: As widely used neuron model in Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs), the Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) model assumes the linear summation of injected currents. However, recent studies have revealed that a biological neuron can integrate inputs nonlinearly and perform computations such as XOR while an LIF neuron cannot. To bridge this gap, we propose the Dendritic LIF (DLIF) model, which incorporates a bilinear dendritic integration rule derived from neurophysiological experiments. At the single-neuron level, we theoretically demonstrate that a DLIF neuron can capture input correlations, enabling it to perform nonlinear classification tasks. At the network level, we prove that DLIF neurons can preserve and propagate correlation structures from the input layer to the readout layer. These theoretical findings are further confirmed by our numerical experiments. Extensive experiments across diverse architectures—including ResNet, VGG, and Transformer—demonstrate that DLIF achieves state-of-the-art performance on static (CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet) and neuromorphic (DVS-Gesture, DVS-CIFAR10) benchmarks, surpassing LIF and other advanced alternatives while maintaining comparable computational cost. This work provides a biologically plausible and computationally powerful spiking neuron model, paving the way for next-generation brain-inspired computing.
